story:
Manco Cápac was born at Tamputoco to Apu Tambo, head of a nomadic ayllu. After his father's death, Manco Cápac led the group's wandering families toward the Cusco valley, defeating three small tribes—the Sahuares, Huallas, and Alcahuisas—and settling in a swampy area between two streams. He founded Cusco, dividing it into four districts, though his people remained small compared to powerful neighboring tribes like the confederated Ayarmacas and Pinaguas, who often attacked the new city. Manco Cápac, and later his son Sinchi Roca, defended Cusco against these enemies. He married his sister Mama Uqllu, and together they had Sinchi Roca, his successor. Manco Cápac died naturally; his mummified body remained in Cusco until ruler Pachacuti later moved it to the Temple of the Sun on Isla del Sol.

In one legend, Manco Cápac (called Ayar Manco) was son of Viracocha, traveling with three brothers and four sisters from Paqariq Tampu, carrying a golden staff given by his father. He eliminated his brothers—turning them to stone or trapping them—to become sole leader, then married his sister Mama Ocllo and fathered Sinchi Roca.

In another legend, Manco Cápac was son of the sun god Inti and moon goddess Mama Killa, brother of Pacha Kamaq. Sent to earth from the cave of Pacaritambo with the golden staff, he and his siblings traveled to Cusco to build a temple honoring Inti.

A third legend says Manco Cápac was son of sorceress Mama Waqu, who enchanted the people of Cusco into naming her queen. She hid her infant son, declared a divine king would emerge from Paqariq Tampu, and after two years revealed Manco Cápac as the new ruler. She then married her son, and they ruled together.

The founder-hero was born at a cave of origin to a tribal chief, head of a nomadic kin-group. After his father's death, the hero led the group's wandering families toward a fertile valley, defeating three small tribes there and settling in a swampy area between two streams. He founded a great city, dividing it into four districts, though his people remained small compared to powerful neighboring tribes, a confederated group who often attacked the new city. The hero, and later his son, defended the city against these enemies. He married his sister, and together they had a son, his successor. The hero died naturally; his mummified body remained in the city until a later ruler moved it to a sacred temple on an island in a great lake.

In one legend, the hero was son of a creator god, traveling with three brothers and four sisters from the cave of origin, carrying a golden staff given by his father. He eliminated his brothers—turning them to stone or trapping them—to become sole leader, then married his sister and fathered his successor.

In another legend, the hero was son of the sun god and moon goddess, brother of another deity. Sent to earth from the cave of origin with the golden staff, he and his siblings traveled to the city to build a temple honoring the sun god.

A third legend says the hero was son of a sorceress, who enchanted the people of the city into naming her queen. She hid her infant son, declared a divine king would emerge from the cave of origin, and after two years revealed the hero as the new ruler. She then married her son, and they ruled together.
title: Manco Cápac
